abstract: Prior work has shown that large language models (LLMs) express implicit biases in high-publicity, one-off decision scenarios such as hiring and intelligence assessment. However, as people increasingly employ autonomous, LLM-powered AI agents that make decisions on their behalf in doing day-to-day tasks, it is of critical importance that we understand how implicit biases, based on sociodemographic assumptions, emerge across a broad milieu of workaday decision scenarios. We used the 17 domains of daily activity in the American Time Use Survey (ATUS) to generate an atlas of 506 decision scenarios in which LLMs --- endowed with personas representing different races, gender identities, and political ideologies --- expressed significant implicit bias. Next, in a crowdsourced audit, 500 participants made 8,010 binary choices about which implicitly biased decision scenarios most deserved further review. We found that participants prioritized decision scenarios that had broad relevance (e.g., about food choices), were high stakes (e.g., about health), and where all members of a simulated sociodemographic group made unanimous decisions (because it was a clear indication of stereotyping). They were less swayed by the magnitude of an observed disparity or the specific ATUS domain the decision scenario represented. When examining the rationale behind their prioritization choices, we found that participants often interpreted disparities as traits of demographic groups and judged whether those traits seemed plausible, often based on their own internalized stereotypes. We discuss implications for building personalized AI agents, digital twins, social simulations, and for using crowdsourced bias audits.
title: A Crowd-Audited Atlas of Implicit Bias in LLM-Powered Agents

abstract: We introduce EJBench, a benchmark of engineering judgement: whether a model can predict how a design behaves at new conditions from a few earlier results, and decide on it. Unlike engineering benchmarks that test whether an agent can operate simulation or CAD software, EJBench is software-agnostic and asks what an engineer would conclude without running a simulation. Its tasks come from a conjugate heat transfer design campaign for battery cold plates, in three families: matching unlabelled test results to their operating points, choosing which stored runs to reveal before signing off a design, and ranking new duties by peak cell temperature. Every answer is taken from a converged simulation, not from an LLM judge. The best of ten frontier models, GPT-6 Astra, scores 0.71, and models state almost the same confidence on tasks they get wrong as on tasks they get right. We also post-train Qwen3.5-9B with LoRA and reinforcement learning, rewarded by the share of answer criteria the simulation results confirm; on the held-out test split its score rises from 0.071 to 0.106. We release the train, validation and test splits, the evaluation harness and the leaderboard.
title: Bookkeeping Is Not Judgement: EJBench, an Engineering Judgement Benchmark Built from a Conjugate Heat Transfer Design Campaign

abstract: Visual artifact tasks test agents' ability to translate task specifications and source materials into outputs that meet practical needs. Evaluation across artifact families helps distinguish broadly applicable authoring capabilities from strengths confined to a particular medium. We introduce VisualArtifactSpec 1.0 (VAS), a benchmark of 211 creation and modification tasks spanning presentations, static graphics, animations and videos, and web interfaces. Each task specifies authoring objectives, source materials, constraints, and deliverables. Existing benchmarks provide limited support for systematically evaluating how authoring choices suit different audiences, purposes, and media across artifact families. VAS evaluates two aspects separately: Task Fulfillment verifies explicit requirements and applicable functionality, while Artifact Performance assesses Content, Organization, Visuals, and Delivery. Task-specific rating anchors instantiate shared criteria for the intended audience, purpose, and medium, with judgments grounded in source materials and artifact inspection records. We evaluate nine model-harness configurations on all 211 tasks. Overall scores range from 42.12 to 70.52, with Artifact Performance accounting for 73.4% of the gap between the highest- and lowest-scoring configurations.
title: VisualArtifactSpec 1.0: Evaluating Visual Artifacts under Task Specifications

abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting enables object-level operations on Gaussian primitives, yet existing segmentation methods are largely trained and evaluated through rendered views. This mismatch can produce accurate rendered masks from incomplete 3D selections since alpha-blended feature supervision concentrates learning on dominant contributors while leaving occluded or low-contribution Gaussians weakly supervised. We propose VODA, a plug-and-play supervision objective that exploits local depth structure to group per-pixel contributors and directly supervises all Gaussians in selected depth clusters, bypassing contribution-weighted gradient delivery. To evaluate volumetric completeness, we introduce Removal-3D, a synthetic object-removal benchmark, and the Removal Depth Error (RDE), a metric comparing predicted and ground-truth depth changes. Across four rendering-based baselines, VODA consistently improves volumetric segmentation on Removal-3D while maintaining or improving performance on LERF and ScanNet. Further analysis shows that VODA recovers lower-contribution Gaussians, while simple gradient reweighting and spatial propagation fail to reproduce comparable gains.
title: The Mask Is Not the Object: Volumetric Supervision for 3D Gaussian Segmentation

abstract: Large language models often produce hallucinated answers, motivating selective prediction policies that abstain on uncertain queries. However, heuristic uncertainty thresholds alone do not provide statistical control of errors among accepted predictions. Linear Expectation Constraints (LEC) reduce selection-conditioned error rate (SCER) calibration to a nonpositive expected linear-loss constraint, but the associated loss is non-monotonic in the acceptance threshold. We construct an exact counterexample under i.i.d. sampling demonstrating that LEC's empirical threshold-selection rule can violate the population SCER target. To address this risk-transfer gap, we introduce Stability-Compensated Linear Expectation Control (SC-LEC), which uses the negative linear risk of a theoretical full-data reference to compensate for threshold-selection instability. For local expansion beyond a safe anchor, we derive two finite-sample certificates: a stability-based certificate exploiting rank crossings and a direct certificate using the structure of threshold expansion to reduce conservatism. With a valid population anchor margin, our certificate conditions ensure finite-sample marginal SCER control, and independent margin certification further provides a $1-δ$ high-probability guarantee for this calibration-averaged control. Experiments on CommonsenseQA, ARC-Challenge, and TriviaQA show useful retention gains beyond the same certified anchor, while revealing conservative behavior in small-margin regimes.
title: Stability-Compensated Threshold Calibration for Selection-Conditioned Risk Control in Large Language Models

abstract: Fine-tuning a small typed decision model on one user's email labels did not clear the margin we pre-registered over a logistic regression trained on the same labels. In earlier work, about two hundred labels and a TF-IDF logistic regression had the highest point accuracy on this inbox, though not significantly above the best hosted model; we ask whether the same labels, given to a decision model, close the gap. A first registered study, on a generic 4B base with cross-validation and message type only, stayed below the baseline at every label budget (-1.8 to -7.3 points). The main study was registered before any fine-tuning run: a fixed test set of 135 emails never used for selection, LoRA adapters on the public Tev1-0.8B and Tev1-4B decision models, nested subsets of 50 to 587 labels, two seeds and five decision fields on a free T4 GPU. Four of its five hypotheses are refuted--two in the fine-tunes' favour--and one is confirmed for one model. On message type the 4B model misses the registered three-point margin at 400 labels (+2.6) and passes it with all 587 (+3.3); with all labels both models are above the baseline by +0.7 and +3.3 points, where one email is 0.74 points and a 95% interval is about 15 points wide, and the 4B model is clearly ahead in type macro-F1 (0.581 vs. 0.406). On the three action switches the baseline is ahead at every label budget for both models (0.931 vs. 0.904 and 0.899 mean accuracy with all labels), at under a millisecond per question against 306 and 1681 ms. The 0.8B type curve barely improves after 300 labels and then falls. The baseline never predicts the two rarest classes (7 offers and 8 spam in the training pool); the fine-tuned models find spam in some runs, not consistently across seeds. We list the explanations we did not test and say when a new attempt would be worth making. Scripts are public; weights and emails are not.
title: Train After You Measure: a Pre-Registered Learning Curve for Fine-Tuning Typed Decision Models on One User's Labels

abstract: Multilingual speakers choose languages by topic and conversation partner. Large language models (LLMs) support these languages unequally. Research on code-switching with conversational AI has mostly examined bilingual pairs of well-resourced languages. In Curaçao and Aruba, many people use Dutch, English, Spanish, and the low-resource Creole Papiamentu/o. In a preregistered study, 42 university students held two five-minute chatbot conversations, one about university life and one about local food and culture. Surveys assessed language background, AI use, and switching comfort. 20 international students in Curaçao formed a comparison sample. Participants switched between turns and rarely mixed languages within a message. English dominated both conversations. Participants switched more often in the cultural conversation, where Papiamentu/o and Spanish rose from 15% to 24% of messages. Self-reports showed no lower comfort switching with the chatbot than with a person. Conversational agents must follow turn-by-turn language changes and handle local low-resource languages well.
title: Beyond Bilingual: Studying Quadrilingual Code-Switching with Conversational AI

abstract: Why does symmetric sum-pooling (DeepSets) predict ground-state potentials to sub-meV accuracy, yet fail for correlated wavefunctions and excited states? Sum-pooling is a mean-field (Hartree) model: its $O(1/N)$ off-diagonal Jacobian suffices for nearsighted ground-state energies, but erases nonlocal two-body correlations. We show that self-attention is a real-space Dyson iteration whose Boltzmann (softmax) kernel acts as a two-body self-energy. Because physical Hamiltonians act pairwise, Löwdin's 2-RDM theorem and the Galitskii--Migdal relation guarantee that iterating a two-body propagator captures the full energetics of correlated matter. When fitting a fractal backflow determinant, DeepSets blurs the nodal surface onto a mean-field envelope, whereas self-attention recovers the fractal attractor. Seen through this lens, the unreasonable effectiveness of attention is not an accident; in a universe built from pairwise interactions, two-body attention is all you need.
title: Self-attention is a Dyson equation for many-body machine learning

abstract: MegNIST is a benchmark dataset for developing and evaluating machine learning methods for inner speech decoding from magnetoencephalography (MEG). The dataset comprises 12,000 trials of a single participant imagining speaking the digits zero through nine, recorded across four sessions. Each trial contains 306-channel MEG recordings sampled at 250 Hz, preprocessed using signal space separation, filtering, and downsampling. Data are provided as pre-defined training (10,000 trials), validation (1,000 trials), and test (1,000 trials) splits, with entire experimental runs assigned to each split to preserve temporal independence. The dataset is available in both BIDS format for neuroimaging analysis and as serialised tensors for machine learning workflows. Baseline classification results demonstrate that imagined digits can be decoded significantly above chance. Standardised splits, validated baselines, example code, and a PyTorch-compatible loader in the pnpl Python library enable straightforward integration with machine learning frameworks, lowering barriers for researchers to rapidly develop and benchmark inner speech decoding methods for non-invasive brain-computer interfaces.
title: MegNIST, A Benchmark for Non-Invasive Inner Speech Decoding

abstract: Modeling large multi-agent systems poses challenges for trajectory inference and parameter identification, as network size and coupling increase computational demands and partial observations require reconstructing unobserved states. We propose MAS-PINN, a neural-network architecture with a tailored training algorithm for a physics-informed learning framework that leverages the network topology and the agents' similarity to reduce computational and memory costs of simulating and identifying multi-agent systems. Its architecture represents agent trajectories through shared temporal features and agent-specific coefficients. Training alternates between learning features, fitting coupled trajectories, and estimating physical parameters. A matrix-free update exploits local interactions to fit trajectories without forming large global matrices. Experiments on Lorenz rings, Lotka--Volterra networks, and Rössler oscillators show improved trajectory and parameter accuracy over baselines, including inference in large systems and identification under partial observations or unknown topology, alongside substantial computational savings in coefficient fitting.
title: Efficient Modeling of Multi-Agent Systems via Structure-Aware Physics-Informed Learning

abstract: AI systems for creative media generation expand human capabilities yet risk diminishing human agency. A core problem is anchoring, where the user's thinking becomes anchored to a polished, generated artifact, shifting the user's role from active authoring to reactive editing. We propose pre-generation belief controls that can empower creators to inspect, revise, and steer the AI's interpretation before any media is generated, so that the initial anchor is set by the human. We formalize four design principles and instantiate them in the Proactive Co-Creator (PaCC), a system for early-stage conceptual ideation and prototyping that proactively surfaces its assumptions and uncertainty through clarifications, belief graphs, and media attributes, inviting users to shape the AI's beliefs before generating the final outcome. Using PaCC as a design probe in a small-scale, single-arm exploratory user study, we observed that participants reported directionally positive sense of agency and process control relative to their familiar prompt-based AI tools, noting that surfaced assumptions helped them think through details they had overlooked, whereas their feelings about ownership and authorship diverged
title: Shaping AI's Beliefs Before It Generates: Human Sense of Agency in Creative AI

abstract: A harness turns a model into a system that completes tasks: it builds the prompt, exposes tools and decides when work is done. Harness comparisons hold the model fixed. Model comparisons hold the harness fixed. We vary both: five shipped harnesses, 18 artifact-producing tasks, four locally deployable open-weight models from 0.75B to 4.7B and a 35.5B anchor, with one deterministic checker scoring all 360 ladder cells. The completion-controlling harness, Mingbird, has the highest mean at every size. Of four pre-registered paired contrasts, two survive Holm correction, at 0.75B and 4.7B. Thirteen of sixteen paired intervals exclude zero under the deployment reading, with leads from 0.075 over the strongest rival to 0.819 over the weakest. The completion gate is not the carrier: disabling all six executable checks moves the mean by +0.080, +0.117, +0.003 and -0.004, every interval including zero, and only at 1.9B does disabling it create empty runs. Removing one repeat-blocking rule alone costs 0.411 at 0.75B and leaves eight of eighteen tasks with no artifact. The harness effect is a progress effect: it decides whether a run leaves anything on disk. Of 357 usable cells, 127 leave none of their declared artifacts and 85 of those exit normally, so a scorer that reads exit status credits work that was never written. Whether the effect grows or shrinks with size, four rungs cannot settle: a floor arm produces a rise, a ceiling a decline, and a cross-family rung a peak.
title: Harness Leverage Across Model Size: A Ladder of Five Local Agent Harnesses from 0.75B to 4.7B

abstract: A popular ideation recipe treats an embedding map of existing work as a guide: pick points far from everything and decode them into ideas. I test four ways such distances could guide ideation against what appeared later. (1) Far random directions are not text: no later item reaches a raw cosine above about 0.10 with one (after centring or whitening, 22 of 24 cells stay out of reach), and an LLM decoder shown a target's neighbours, with score-only feedback, writes those neighbours in all six target sets. A neighbour-free search writes coherent text at median cosine 0.57 and 0.47 to interior gaps, beating the nearest existing item on 15 and 14 of 20, but only 0.07 and 0.06 to far points. (2) On k-means cells of a past-only map, the registered hole score mostly tracks cell size and position; three density-based gap scores forecast which cells grow fastest at or below chance (AUC 0.30 to 0.66) and add nothing to momentum in Steam and arXiv, with patents inconclusive; more isolated new Steam games are slightly better reviewed. (3) LLM continuations of arXiv papers stay closer to the source than papers that cite it, under three user prompts and against proposal rewrites (gpt-4o) and April-December 2023 papers (OLMo). Critique lengthens this step beyond content-free revision, replicated on 150 new papers. Revealing a real follow-up's title turns the ideas by 0.032 along a follow-up-specific direction beyond revision; reviewer, oracle and distance feedback add 0.13, 0.08 and 0.34 of that turn (upper bounds 0.46, 0.46, 0.70), and their turn is not separable from revision or their longer step. (4) For inspiration material graded by distance, no inverted U was detected, on an anticipation margin that tracks format more than content. Original tests were registered before running, follow-ups (thirteen requested in two AI-agent reviews) after the main results; all are dated only by local git commits.
title: Do Embedding-Map Distances Guide LLM Ideation? Four Tests Against What Came Next

abstract: Formal specifications define intended program behavior and underpin verification, but writing them in theorem provers such as Lean is slow and expertise-intensive, making specification a major bottleneck to scaling formally correct code. Autoformalization from natural-language problems is promising, yet training specification models requires scalable feedback on whether generated specifications capture intended behavior. Prior approaches obtain this feedback through explicit proofs or separately implemented code with formal correspondence proofs, both expensive. We introduce AuXSpec, a Lean framework that pairs declarative postconditions with executable counterparts, obtained through type class resolution when possible and otherwise defined separately with an equivalence proof. Test cases can then evaluate declarative specifications by execution, letting us use agreement as a reinforcement-learning reward. Using AuXSpec, we synthesize 3,037 LeetCode problems and expand training to 19.5K samples through expert iteration on Codeforces. Experiments show that training Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.8-27B with the execution-based reward improves SpecGen pass@4 on AuXSpec-Test 0.7% $\to$ 82.7% and 14.3% $\to$ 84.3%, and the 27B model outperforms all frontier models. On the out-of-domain Verina benchmark with its original prompts, both models improve 7.0% $\to$ 90.5% and 21.9% $\to$ 90.5% and surpass VeriSpecGen-30B-A3B, the prior state of the art among open-source specification models, on pass@1 (theirs 47.6% vs. ours 73.7% and 84.5%) and pass@4 (theirs 63.9% at pass@10 vs. ours 90.5%). We release the weights of the trained 9B and 27B models and the 3,037 problems with test cases, including the 300-problem AuXSpec-Test benchmark with expert review and correctness proofs for future evaluation. Models and data: https://huggingface.co/collections/eth-algopt/auxspec. Website: https://auxspec.org
title: AuXSpec: Learning to Autoformalize Program Specifications via Executable Postconditions

abstract: Grading student responses is costly and time-consuming. Moreover, human annotators are prone to bias, fatigue, and rater drift, which further limits grading reliability. Various methods have been employed to develop automated essay scoring (AES) systems to reduce these costs and address bias-related issues. These methods range from early text-feature-based systems to current machine-learning and transformer-based models. Specifically, large language models (LLMs) offer the potential to streamline the development of AES systems. However, they are subject to well-known limitations, such as hallucinations and prompt sensitivity. This creates a need to explore the potential of a mixed-methods approach that leverages the synergies among individual LLMs through ensemble formation. We evaluate the potential of ensembles of LLMs to match human-rater agreement when grading student responses in economics and medical education across 103 criteria. We use 631 German-language responses and corresponding human ratings by 2 to 5 annotators from a previously conducted assessment. We experiment with 523 rubric-based prompt configurations across 15 open-weight LLMs and assess their consistency with human raters using Krippendorff's alpha for inter-annotator agreement (IAA) and the Alternative Annotator Test (alt-test). Our results show that replacing one human rater with the best-performing LLM--prompt configuration maintains or improves IAA for 91 of the 103 criteria and that LLMs pass the alt-test for 90 criteria. Our findings suggest that current state-of-the-art LLMs can support AES of German responses in economics and medical education, reducing human workload and enabling faster processing, while validation against human ratings remains necessary.
title: Rubric-Based AES with LLM Ensembles: Scoring of Student Responses in Critical Online Reasoning Using Ensembles of LLMs

abstract: Machine learning models for chemical reaction prediction are usually evaluated by endpoint accuracy, but endpoint correctness alone does not reveal how a model represents chemical transformation or why it fails. We introduce UniRxnAxis, a unified forward-retrosynthesis framework that models both tasks as direction-conditioned endpoint redistribution in a shared latent space. By aligning source states, transformed states, and encoded target endpoints, UniRxnAxis enables directional auditing of learned latent updates. This shared latent geometry allows the learned displacement (from the encoder source state $S_0$ to the decoder-facing transformed state $S_1$) to be decomposed into an endpoint-parallel component and an endpoint-orthogonal residual, which we call emergent steering. Our evaluation shows that emergent steering is functionally important: in retrosynthesis, it recovers most of the model's utility, remains effective under random, shuffled, and prototype controls, and directly affects which bond edits are promoted or suppressed. The residual-over-parallel ordering persists across alignment strengths, after decoder-interface calibration, against angle-matched random axes, and in a second graph-edit architecture, although its magnitude depends on the reference axis and optimization. The decomposition also supports a proxy taxonomy of model-side failures, showing how reaction models can be audited beyond endpoint accuracy.
title: Emergent Steering Beyond Endpoint Alignment in Chemical Reaction Models

abstract: Weight-space programming removes the thinking loops of a small reasoning model by a rank-one edit W' = W + u v^T of an MLP output matrix, where u is a loop direction and v is the solution of a sparse Linear Program (LP) over the neuron activations. We investigate whether the LP is needed. We replace it by a sort: we take the 8 neurons whose activation has the smallest coefficient of variation, and give them equal shares of the push that the LP solution realizes. On Qwen3.5-0.8B the sorted edit scores 67.0% on 1000 problems (MATH-500 and GSM8K) against 67.4% for the LP edit and 9.5% for the unedited model; the paired difference is -0.4 points, with 95% confidence interval [-2.9, +2.1], inside a non-inferiority margin of 5 points declared before the runs. On three further sampling seeds the difference is -0.6 points, interval [-2.0, +0.8], and -0.8 points, interval [-2.3, +0.6], when the dose is set without the LP. The sort does not solve the LP, but the neurons it shares with the LP solution carry most of its mean push. The outcome is that, on this model, the edit acts as a nearly constant bias along u.
title: Just sort it! A note on the LP behind rank-one anti-loop edits

abstract: The electronic Schrödinger equation encodes a molecule's electronic structure and quantum properties, but solving it scales exponentially with the number of electrons. Solving this equation with neural-network variational Monte Carlo (VMC) has reached chemical accuracy on the ground state of small molecules; extending this success to excited states is constrained by two existing paradigms. Penalty-based methods need $K$ Laplacians per step but require tuning the overlap-penalty weights against the energy gaps they aim to compute. Natural excited states VMC (NES-VMC) is penalty-free, but it combines the $K$ ansatzes into one determinant, whose local energy requires $K^2$ Laplacians per step. We resolve this trade-off via low-rank approximation (LoRA) reparameterization of the rank-$K$ variational objective. The reparameterized objective admits a VMC-compatible stochastic gradient estimator via MCMC sampling from the per-state Born densities, and a sequential nesting scheme recovers the lowest $K$ eigenstates in eigenvalue order. The resulting algorithm, NestedLoRA-VMC, inherits a global optimality guarantee from the LoRA principle. On the first-row atoms Li through Ne at $K=10$, its accuracy is comparable to that of NES-VMC and of a state-of-the-art penalty-based method.
title: Variational Monte Carlo for Quantum Excited States via Nested Low-Rank Approximation

abstract: In particle physics, discrepancies between experimental measurements and Standard Model (SM) predictions are commonly interpreted within new theoretical models. In this context, the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) provides a general framework encompassing a broad class of models. However, exploring the enormous space of possible SMEFT operators rapidly becomes a challenging combinatorial problem: many operators can contribute simultaneously to different observables, their effects are correlated, and distinct operator combinations can provide comparably good descriptions of the data. In this work, we formulate the exploration of the SMEFT operator space as a sequential decision-making problem using reinforcement learning (RL). Our RL agent employs a lightweight actor-critic architecture with approximately 40K trainable parameters in total. Rather than searching for a single best-fit theory, our method is designed to discover a diverse set of high-quality theory hypotheses. We test the method in a complex phenomenological environment comprising 132 observables across several sectors of particle physics, including 24 measurements that deviate from their SM predictions by more than $1.5σ$. We show that the learned RL policy efficiently constructs multi-operator theories that substantially improve the global fit. Comparisons with independent random-subset and random-sequential searches demonstrate the ability of the RL policy to navigate this large combinatorial space. Our results establish RL as a systematic framework for exploring diverse patterns of new physics (NP) interactions within SMEFT.
title: A Reinforcement Learning Method to Navigate SMEFT Operator Space

abstract: Reasoning-enhanced generative recommendation (GR) has attracted increasing attention for leveraging the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to improve next-item prediction. However, existing methods primarily optimize reasoning through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with rule-based rewards determined by final recommendation performance, which faces two key limitations: (i) unmeasured predictive contributions within reasoning, where the predictive contributions of individual reasoning steps are not directly reflected in optimization signals, and (ii) weakly discriminative learning signals within groups, where different reasoning trajectories within the group often receive indistinguishable rewards, limiting effective policy optimization. In this paper, we propose GainReason, a simple yet effective training framework that optimizes reasoning through Predictive Gain (PG). Specifically, PG measures changes in target Semantic ID (SID) log-likelihood induced by individual reasoning sentences, providing contribution-aware and discriminative rewards. We further theoretically establish the alignment between expected PG and the recommendation ranking objective. Building on this signal, we develop PG-based Reasoning Optimization (PGRO) to optimize reasoning generation with sentence-level rewards, supported by a custom causal attention mechanism for efficient PG computation. Additionally, an auxiliary PG-based Reasoning Utilization (PGRU) task adaptively strengthens reasoning-conditioned prediction to complement PGRO. Extensive experiments on three public benchmarks demonstrate that GainReason consistently outperforms competitive baselines and achieves substantial performance gains from reasoning.
title: Learning to Reason with Predictive Gains for Generative Recommendation

abstract: Researchers at MIT recently reported that GPT-6 Astra, a frontier large language model (LLM), can write the weights of small neural networks directly in a single reply, and can read the raw weights of small networks to say what they were trained to do. In a three-day sprint, we replicated and extended these results. Our four findings: (1) Writing weights reproduces. Astra's networks for the game Breakout scored 514, 550 and 307 (versus MIT's 517), and scored just as well on two modified versions of Breakout. Claude Opus 5.5 can also write working networks, but often runs out of output tokens. (2) What is new is translating programs into weights. Earlier models could write a good policy as code a generation before they could write network weights, and the networks the models write behave like compiled programs: two models independently decompiled Astra's Breakout network into Python matching its actions in all tested states. On classifying handwritten digits, Astra's networks scored 50% on average, below a simple classifier (82%). (3) Reading weights is mostly reading the input layer. Astra and Opus 5.5 identify which game a network plays almost perfectly, but on three new games we designed and trained ourselves, Astra recovered where things are on the board, while mostly missing how the game works. (4) Auditing from weights alone is possible but shallow. Without executing code, Astra picked out a small language model poisoned during training in 10 of 10 runs, one poisoned by extra training afterwards in 7 of 10, and a malicious adapter in 23 of 32 cases, but never identified the trigger or malicious behaviour. Open-weight models lag behind. From this early study, we conclude that LLMs can read and write small networks, but that this currently amounts to compiling hand-designed programs and reading the layout of the input layer. It is a promising but early tool for interpretability.
title: Replicating and Extending Weight-Space Programming: Frontier LLMs Compile Programs into Weights and Read Input Layers

abstract: We discuss the Journal of the American Statistical Association (JASA) discussion paper "Deep Fréchet Regression" and explore an alternative perspective based on conditional flow matching. We propose learning covariate-dependent transport directly within the response space, avoiding separate manifold learning and reverse mapping. This perspective offers a potentially more flexible framework for incorporating geometric structure and modeling full conditional distributions.
title: Comments on "Deep Fréchet Regression"

abstract: AI assistants are becoming part of how knowledge workers think and perform, accumulating the prompts, exemplars, memory and interaction histories that encode a worker's professional judgment. This infrastructure typically runs under employer or platform control. We name the resulting process expertise capture, the absorption of worker-applied knowledge and judgment into AI resources under organizational control. We develop a framework of contribution forms, technical residences and transformation families, and show that how far a contribution can be attributed, separated and revoked depends on where it resides and how it has been transformed, properties fixed by system design long before any dispute arises. When a worker departs, the organization retains a capability shaped by their judgment while the worker loses access to it, and the asymmetry compounds as contributions move from inspectable artifacts into derivatives, learned components and successor systems. We outline three measures, write-time provenance, extraction of separable contributions and an executable exit procedure, that make an agreed allocation technically performable, and make explicit what cannot be separated at all.
title: Expertise capture in workplace AI

abstract: Question answering over ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing scenes poses a tension for multimodal large language models: global overviews obscure small objects and local attributes, whereas detailed crops consume substantial context. Compressing inspected crops into short sequences of continuous visual latents offers a compact memory once crop tokens are discarded, yet diagnostic studies on natural images find that models often ignore latent content, leaving unclear whether compact latents can retain fine-grained targets lost in downsampled UHR remote sensing scenes. To isolate evidence retention from region selection, we encode high-resolution crops into latent memory tokens for frozen backbones and evaluate both their predictive utility and content dependence. Across two generations of Qwen-VL on LRS-GRO, a 64-token memory achieves 7.6- to 9.9-fold compression of retained crop tokens and improves accuracy by 2.5 to 4.8 percentage points over the downsampled global image alone, recovering most of the high-resolution crop gain with consistent behavior on XLRS-Bench. Substituting memory from another image or another region of the same scene reduces accuracy by 5.8 to 7.4 percentage points and yields lower accuracy than removing memory altogether, demonstrating that predictions depend on the encoded regional evidence. Restoring the source crop within the same model reduces the accuracy loss caused by zeroing or removing memory. These findings establish that compact visual latents retain useful local evidence in UHR remote sensing and identify evidence availability as a key factor governing their contribution.
title: Out of Sight, Into Memory: Compact Visual Latents Retain Local Evidence in Ultra-High-Resolution Remote Sensing

abstract: Annotators from different demographic backgrounds often disagree in systematic ways due to varying lived experiences, cultural contexts, and their relationship to the content. When such disagreement occurs, one group's perspective may sometimes warrant prioritization because they hold an epistemically advantaged standpoint or bear greater stake in the outcome. For example, when assessing toxicity of posts on social media, it may be important to prioritize a targeted group's viewpoint. We propose a Stakeholder-Aware Joint Multi-Task Learning (SAJ-MTL) framework to jointly model demographic disagreement both across- and within- annotator groups. The model uses conditional gradient routing to handle sparsity induced by group-conditional labeling, and parameterization supports customized weighting of groups in different task settings. SAJ-MTL improves group-level performance in toxicity detection through better context-aware understanding of demographic-sensitive content. Only annotator group-membership information is required, which is more practical than existing methods requiring more privacy-invasive individual-level annotator details. Our scalable architecture is also computationally efficient to support large-scale deployment.
title: A Scalable Multi Task Learning Framework for Modeling Demographic Disagreements in Annotation Tasks

abstract: Weight Factorization (WF) methods aim to reduce a model's latency, memory, or both. These typically decompose a pretrained model into two or more factors that approximate the original model weights with fewer parameters and floating point operations (FLOPs). However, translating fewer FLOPs into reduced latency is challenging for WF methods in practice due to overhead introduced by replacing a single large weight matrix with multiple smaller ones. To address this, we propose Balanced Twin Weight Factorization (BTWF), which uses the unique structure of factorized models to simultaneously lower latency and increase learning capacity. Specifically, BTWF operates in the shared basis WF setting, where two or more layers are decomposed into a shared basis matrix and a layer-specific mixing matrix. If these shared layers have the same input (i.e., are twins), then we need only perform this shared forward pass once, reducing inference time. However, twin layers are often of varying sizes, and methods from prior work tend to favor the larger layer. In contrast, our approach boosts performance by combining Factor Component Balancing (FCB), which ensures every shared member is well represented in the selected factors, with Block Contribution Balancing (BCB), which considers downstream model effects. Further, we also show that an overparameterized BTWF, where some layer's factors result in higher FLOPs than the original during training, can boost task performance without additional resources at test time. Experiments on six models over nine benchmarks show BTWF obtains a 2-6% gain over the state-of-the-art without expensive finetuning (1-3.5% gain with it) at comparable computational costs.
title: Balanced Twin Weight Factorization for Efficient MLLMs

abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) leverages a model of the environment, used for planning and generating samples without interacting with the real world. Motivated by evidence that informed initialization significantly improves the efficiency of MBRL, we propose TDec-Init, an algorithm to warm-start neural dynamics models using transition Jacobians. Using a decoupling algorithm based on the decomposition of a tensor of stacked Jacobian samples, we recover weights and flexible nonlinearities, and use them to initialize a feedforward neural network. In the low-data regime, we show on several benchmark environments that our approach outperforms random initialization and value training, and either matches or outperforms Sobolev training, while requiring fewer training steps between episodes.
title: Warm Starting Neural Dynamics Models From Few Jacobian Samples

abstract: Generative data augmentation adds samples from generative models to a classifier's training set. Many influential studies use generators pre-trained on large external datasets, and so mix the value of synthetic data with knowledge transferred through pretraining. We study the case without external data, where each generator learns only from the classifier's own training set, and ask when and why adding generated samples to that training set raises or lowers the classifier's test accuracy. We train classifiers with four backbones on six datasets, two of them medical, adding samples from four generators. We bound the excess risk of a classifier trained with synthetic data, that is, how far its population risk can lie above the minimum risk within its hypothesis class. The bound charges synthetic data for the total variation distance between the real and generated distributions and credits synthetic data for a larger training set. The gain from adding synthetic data, the fall in population risk, is at most the excess risk of the real-only classifier, which trains on the real images alone. Read through the bound, the experiments suggest that synthetic data help most when our classifiers detect only a small discrepancy between the generated and real data and the real-only classifier has room to improve, and that synthetic data help little or hurt when the detected discrepancy is large. Generators with a larger lower bound on the total variation distance, a bound that we estimate from our own classifiers, tend to help less on five of the six datasets, and on the CIFAR datasets the most accurate backbone gains the least. The bound gives these directions but not the size of the largest gains, most of which traditional augmentation also reaches at the same number of optimizer steps.
title: Generative Data Augmentation Without External Data: An Empirical and Theoretical Study on Deep Networks

abstract: Physics-informed operator learning trains neural operators on the residual of a parametric partial differential equation (PDE) instead of labeled solution data, but its reliability depends on a variationally correct residual: one that is equivalent to the error in a norm dictated by the equation, the PDE-compliant norm. For nonlinear equations written as first-order systems, we prove that the first-order system least-squares residual is equivalent to the error in this norm near a solution branch if the linearized residual is stable and the residual derivative is Lipschitz continuous, possibly in a norm stronger than the error norm. We verify these conditions for monotone reaction, solution- and gradient-dependent diffusion, and compressible Neo-Hookean hyperelasticity. The stability mechanisms vary across these classes, as do the regions where the equivalence holds, from arbitrary bounded sets to a neighborhood of the branch. In a conforming finite element space, we show that the loss excess of a state near the finite element solution is equivalent to its squared distance from that solution. We use this loss to train a reduced basis neural operator with values in this space, with solution snapshots needed only for the basis and the loss and its symbolically derived gradient assembled by the finite element library. At inference, this loss estimates the error. Numerically, the square root of the loss excess tracks the error within factors comparable to those of the linear case, and the operator achieves higher accuracy in the PDE-compliant norm than grid-based baselines evaluated in the same finite element space.
title: Variationally correct physics-informed operator learning for nonlinear partial differential equations

abstract: Constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs) typically bound expected cumulative cost from an initial state. Such a guarantee can be insufficient when a policy must remain feasible after every history it may encounter. We introduce \emph{subprocess-constrained MDPs} (S-CMDPs), which require the expected discounted cost of each continuation, conditional on any reachable history, to satisfy a bound determined by the current state. This stronger requirement changes the structure and complexity of the problem: we show that stationary policies can be strictly suboptimal, and finding even an approximately optimal stationary policy is NP-hard. We adapt a recently introduced value-set iteration framework to show that history-dependent policies surprisingly overcome both obstacles. Our polynomial-time algorithm represents such a policy implicitly: its expected reward is within $ε$ of the optimal feasible value, it violates each subprocess cost bound by at most $δ$, and its action distribution can be computed in polynomial time for any given history.
title: Subprocess-Constrained Markov Decision Processes

abstract: Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDSs) must incrementally adapt to emerging attacks, even when only a limited amount of labeled network traffic is available. Consequently, Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning (FSCIL)-based NIDSs have gained growing attention. However, existing FSCIL-based NIDSs are highly vulnerable to label noise in newly-observed attack classes. To address this limitation, we propose NAFN, a noise-aware FSCIL-based NIDS framework that reduces the impact of mislabeled data during incremental adaptation. NAFN consists of two components: (i) Noise Detection, which identifies and removes mislabeled biflows using noise-detection algorithms, and (ii) Feature Sampling, which estimates class-conditional embeddings from clean biflows, calibrates them with base-class statistics, and resamples synthetic features to recover the original biflow count. The framework follows the Rethink Few-Shot (RFS) teacher-student paradigm with lightweight nearest-neighbor or logistic regression classifiers, and various pretraining & memory selection strategies. Experiments on CSE-CIC-IDS2018, Edge-IIoT, and IoT-NID datasets show that NAFN effectively preserves prior knowledge and maintains strong incremental performance even under 50% label noise, consistently improving new-class F1-scores over non-denoised baselines, up to +52%, while being time-efficient and robust in cross-network and high-noise incremental settings. The implementation is publicly available to foster reproducibility.
title: Network Intrusion Detection Adaptability under Spurious Labels: A Noise-Aware Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning Framework

abstract: Higher education is confronting an academic-integrity challenge unlike any in its history. Students can now outsource homework, take-home assignments, and online examinations to large language models (LLMs) that complete them in seconds. Existing research on evaluating LLM performance on academic assessments has focused largely on standardized examinations, or on questions from college-level courses drawn from a single discipline. Far less is known about how LLMs perform on college-level assessment questions spanning multiple disciplines, that instructors have purposely designed to be AI-resistant, and about which features of such questions, if any, meaningfully constrain LLM performance. We address this gap by collecting 75 questions from authentic college coursework assessments, spanning 17 disciplines, which were contributed by 37 faculty members from ten U.S. universities and one U.K. university. Of these, 61 questions were intentionally designed by faculty members to be 'LLM-proof', while the remaining 14 questions were sourced from online courses. We then (i) evaluate three state-of-the-art LLMs' ability to correctly answer these questions with and without supplementary course materials; (ii) identify five strategies, through thematic analysis, that faculty used to make their questions harder for LLMs to solve; and (iii) test whether these strategies impact LLMs' ability to answer the questions accurately. Our experimental results show that the best-performing model scored approximately 83% without supplementary course materials and 85% with them, and we observed noteworthy differences across models, answer formats, and instructor tweaking strategies. We discuss implications for assessment design, academic-integrity policy, and the broader ethics of deploying LLMs in educational settings.
title: Generative AI and the Crisis of Higher Education Assessments: Examining 'AI-Proofing' Strategies for College-Level Assessments

abstract: Whether a stored memory helps answer a user's question often depends on world knowledge rather than surface similarity. Jetriever replaces similarity search with full-pool utility scoring: given a query, it uses Jev, an LLM-derived System One decision model, to score every stored memory for the probability that it is useful to the answer, ranking the memory pool directly by those probabilities. On InMind's 125 indirect-query tasks, Jetriever places the gold exchange first in 84.8% of cases (versus 1.6% for BM25 and 0.0% for MiniLM with user-turn indexing) and reaches 76.0% end-to-end Application, compared with at most 16.0% across published retrieval and memory systems. A controlled 20-question comparison disentangles recognizing implicit evidence from ranking it properly: Jev and Qwen3.5-9B both recover 90% of gold exchanges within the top 50 (versus 30% for the BERT-based decision model Laya), yet at rank 1 Jev reaches 85% while Qwen3.5-9B drops to 40%. On a dimension-proportional random sample of 60 MemoryAgentBench questions, Jetriever raises the four-dimension average from 44.3% (ReFind) to 55.4%, at a mean retrieval cost of USD 0.00834 per InMind query and USD 0.03103 per MAB query. Together, these results show that effective utility retrieval hinges on combining broad world knowledge, calibrated ranking probabilities, and affordable full-pool evaluation.
title: Jetriever: Shifting Agent Memory Retrieval from Similarity to Utility

abstract: Interactive video world models enable exploration through text and camera controls, yet direct object interaction requires finer control. Hands provide a natural interface, but translating continuous hand movements into coherent visual responses remains challenging because of complex hand-object dynamics and demanding real-time computation. To address these challenges, we introduce LynnReal-Hand, a hand-controlled video world model that unifies precise interaction modeling with efficient streaming generation. We curate 100K interaction clips spanning diverse real and synthetic environments and develop hand-aware supervision to improve fine-grained hand motions and object interactions. Building on this foundation, we learn a causal flow map for few-step generation and introduce region-aware score distillation that combines complementary video and image priors to refine interaction dynamics and visual appearance. To further reduce inference latency, we propose Ultra-Fast-VAE, a compact video decoder that preserves high reconstruction fidelity with substantially lower computational cost. Extensive evaluations on HandBench demonstrate superior hand-following accuracy and visual quality compared with existing approaches. Our full-sequence model achieves an FVD of 181.67 and a MANO Dice score of 93.02, while the three-step causal model maintains a MANO Dice score of 92.49. For real-time interaction, 540p streaming on a single H200 reaches 18.03 FPS with 741ms latency and an optimized peak GPU memory footprint of only 34.89GB. We will release the datasets, model weights, and the full training and inference code to support research on hand-controlled video world models.
title: LynnReal-Hand: Unlocking World Interaction with Hand Control

abstract: Electrical Power and Energy Systems face hybrid threats that combine cyber intrusions, physical sabotage and climate-driven stress, and routinely outpace today's siloed monitoring stacks. We present RESILAGENT, a concept architecture organised around three operational pillars, Sensing & Data Intelligence, Resilience Analytics & Reporting, and Incident Response & Recovery, mediated by a Cloud-based Orchestrator and exercised through a closed Detect-Simulate-Decide-Sign loop. The framework fuses agentic artificial intelligence and multimodal large language models for cross-modal detection, real-time digital twins for what-if simulation, and a permissioned blockchain anchor for tamper-evident threat intelligence and CER/NIS2-aligned evidence. We instantiate it on two scenarios, a transmission operator under coordinated cyber compromise, sabotage and heatwave, and a distribution operator under a supply-chain compromise during a storm, and report an IEEE-bus micro-benchmark that quantifies each pillar through false-data-injection attack detection, cyber-physical fusion lift, N-1 contingency screening and anchor cost.
title: RESILAGENT: A Three-Pillar Architecture for Cyber-Physical Resilience in Electrical Power and Energy Systems

abstract: We introduce a framework for differentiable exact learning that couples an unbounded external environment to a state-tracking neural controller, which we train on policy-trajectory observations (PTOs): expert behavior traces that expose observations and actions while hiding internal states. In addition to the learning framework, we introduce Differentiable Finite-State Transducers (DFSTs) which use multilinear updates, support log-parallel training, and emulate arbitrary finite-state controllers, yielding computational universality through environmental interaction. From tiny training datasets, compact DFSTs achieve extreme length generalization on arithmetic and universal-simulation tasks. We replicate the success of DFSTs on RNNs and GRUs, thereby supporting a broader learning recipe: State-Tracking Controller + Unbounded External Environment + PTOs = Extreme Length Generalization. Beyond length generalization, our metric-extraction protocol recovers interpretable discrete controllers from trained DFSTs, which we prove equivalent to the target arithmetic and universal-simulation algorithms. Furthermore, for our Softmax DFST models, simply taking $\mathrm{argmax}$ over the transition probabilities yields discrete controllers which provably exactly perform universal Turing-machine simulation and binary arithmetic. Proving exact learning for the neural controllers requires assumptions, which we empirically support. We make our code, training recipes, model weights, and proof checkers publicly available at https://github.com/fanagor/DEL.
title: Differentiable Exact Learning

abstract: Vision--language agents generate descriptions, decisions, and instructions that may be reused by users, downstream agents, and automated workflows, creating a need for provenance mechanisms that support content authenticity and post-deployment auditing without unnecessarily degrading response quality. We present a risk-aware semantic watermarking framework that combines predictive uncertainty with a zero-shot multimodal relevance-risk proxy to allocate watermark strength during decoding. A single risk penalty $λ$ exposes a continuous operating frontier, allowing deployment-time selection of a detection--quality trade-off without model retraining. At a selected operating point, mean watermark strength is reduced by approximately 59.4\% relative to fixed-strength watermarking, while perplexity change falls from 0.3634 to 0.1689 and clean/paraphrased ROC-AUC reaches 0.9552/0.9459. A matched-strength analysis shows that this advantage reflects the allocation policy rather than lower average intervention: at comparable mean strength, risk-constrained allocation achieves substantially higher ROC-AUC than fixed, entropy-only, and criticality-only policies, identifying it as detection-efficient rather than quality-dominant. We further show that threshold calibration on finite samples produces substantial false-positive-rate drift, motivating calibration variance reporting as standard practice for auditable provenance.
title: Detection-Efficient Watermarking for Vision--Language Agents via Risk-Constrained Strength Allocation

abstract: Cross-border cyber attacks on European SMEs and critical-infrastructure operators expose a structural cyber-resilience gap: cybersecurity (threat sharing, detection, response), compliance (framework assessment, certification) and digital forensics (cross-jurisdictional evidence) are jointly regulated by NIS2, the CRA, GDPR and the LED, yet their tooling evolved in silos and rarely interoperates across Member States. The EU-funded CYBER-BRIDGE project integrates the three domains under one architecture and a hash-chained evidence layer: AI-driven CTI sharing with ENISA-aligned notification, multi-framework assessments with retrieval-augmented advisory, and RFC 3161-anchored custody with lawful GDPR/LED exchange, all aligned with MITRE ATT&CK. A sanitised replica of the back-end image hosts a Cyber-Range for upskilling. The contribution is not the individual tools but the reconciliation mechanism that lets one incident produce, from a single evidence record, a cross-border CTI advisory, the regulatory notifications its deadlines demand and a re-verifiable forensic pack; we set out why binding three differently regulated evidence regimes onto one record is non-trivial and how the shared evidence layer resolves the resulting tensions. This paper introduces the project's scope, requirements, pilots, architecture and toolkits; quantitative KPIs follow in later deliverables.
title: The CYBER-BRIDGE project: An AI-Powered Platform for Cross-Border Cybersecurity, Compliance and Forensics in the EU

abstract: We develop neural realizations of positive-level Wess-Zumino-Witten models using bosonic Wakimoto and fermionic Fourier-Berezin fields. Level-rank duality connects the charged sectors of the fermionic construction, where explicit neural observables recover conformal block data and enable the transfer of information about unknown correlators between paired theories. We also show that distinct neural presentations of the same continuum current algebra exhibit different finite-width behavior, with approximation accuracy depending on architecture, regulator, and parameter distribution. These results connect the exact mathematical structure of conformal field theory with the expressive and computational properties of neural field theories.
title: Learning from Duality in Neural Network Field Theories

abstract: Recently, the Shapley value has been widely applied in machine learning for feature importance analysis and model explainability. The multilinear extension of games proposed by Owen (1972) expresses the Shapley value as the integral of partial derivatives along the main diagonal of the cube. Direct evaluation of this integral requires exponential-time computation of the partial derivatives. To improve computational efficiency, we propose a sampling-based estimation strategy within Owen's multilinear extension framework, combining stratified sampling with coalition leverage scores. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces computational costs while maintaining explanation accuracy.
title: Leverage-Enhanced Sampling Owen Method for Explainable Artificial Intelligence

abstract: Weighted conformal p-values generalize conformal inference to cases with covariate shift. One way to use them is to pass them to the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure, either to decide which test units to select or to detect outliers. But weighted conformal p-values may not be positively dependent, so we want to know: does BH still control the false discovery rate (FDR) in finite samples? Based on experiments, it appears to, but we prove it doesn't. We give two counterexamples, certified in exact rational arithmetic, where the FDR exceeds its target level $q$. We also identify how large the difference between the FDR and $q$ can be. With $n$ calibration points, $m$ test units and weight ratio $B$, the relative excess $\mathrm{FDR}/q-1$ is bounded by a function of $n$, $m$, $B$ and $q$ that is of order $\sqrt{Bm/(nq)}$ when $Bm/(nq)$ is small. The bound holds for every configuration with $B\le n$ and every $n$. This order can be reached when multiple non-null test units share a common threshold: in a Poisson-limit model, that configuration's excess is $c(q)\sqrt{Bm/(nq)}$ to first order as $B/n\to0$ and then $m\to\infty$. For some fixed distributions with this structure, the excess decreases only like $n^{-1/2}$ as $n$ grows. If every test unit is null, the excess is $O(B/n)$ at fixed $m$, and in certain configurations it grows linearly with $m$. To assist practitioners in judging how large the FDR can be, we turn that bound, which depends only on $n$, $m$, $q$ and $B$, into a lowered BH level with proved finite-sample control, and give a much less conservative rule of thumb that covers every worst case we were able to find but provides no guarantee.
title: Almost Controlled: The FDR of Benjamini-Hochberg on Weighted Conformal p-Values

abstract: Task representations for sequential decision making should describe both an objective and progress toward it. We present an algebraically informed pipeline that uses the relational structure and language semantics of alternating finite automata (AFAs) to learn control features and compile compact execution operators. AND-OR message passing learns task and state vectors; selected configurations define an event-driven Boolean matrix operator. We prove that initial and successor language coverage make its carrier represent the exact residual after every prefix, with a sufficient capacity bound in terms of reachable configurations. Conjunction and disjunction use the same pipeline. Fidelity and composition audits evaluate copied formulas and learned disjunct assignments. In five-policy-seed XLand experiments with larger training pools, pooled execution-state vectors outperform raw carrier bits and task-blind conditioning across three task pools under two rejection rewards. They achieve 77.3\% success on multi-event tasks and 99.4\% on a four-task stratum with 33--128-state minimal DFAs, using 16 operator slots. LetterWorld results show useful residual conditioning alongside a remaining gap to RAD. These results connect algebraically informed representation learning to compact task execution and useful policy conditioning.
title: Tensorized Automata: Algebraically Informed Representation Learning for Sequential Decision Making

abstract: Long-horizon manipulation tasks require a robot to perform a sequence of physical interactions with its environment, typically combining several different skills. Planning such behaviors efficiently is challenging: given a library of parameterized skills, solutions lie in a vast hybrid space of skill sequences and their parameters, and evaluating each candidate skill's feasibility and effect with a high-fidelity world model such as a physics simulator is computationally expensive. MOSAIC, a recent skill-centric approach, lets the skills guide a non-sequential search toward the regions of this space where they are likely to succeed; however, it pays the full cost of simulation for every parameterized skill it considers. In this work, we introduce Lazy-MOSAIC, a lazy planning framework that instead searches over hypothesized skill outcomes. A cheap learned skill-effect world model predicts, in a fraction of a millisecond, a skill's feasibility and the world state it produces. Lazy-MOSAIC then uses these predictions to focus expensive simulation on promising candidate skills and, when a hypothesis is invalidated, repairs only the affected part of the search, while ensuring that every skill in a returned plan is validated in simulation. We evaluate Lazy-MOSAIC on cluttered-shelf retrieval tasks of increasing difficulty and demonstrate it on a physical robot, showing that it plans substantially faster than baselines with fewer simulator queries, while matching or exceeding their success rate in every setting. Visit skill-mosaic.github.io.
title: Lazy-MOSAIC: Accelerating Skill-Centric Manipulation Planning with Learned Skill-Effect World Models

abstract: Mean pairwise cosine similarity between transformer embeddings is a standard measure of whether online discourse is converging under generative AI. When the embeddings are mean-pooled outputs of an encoder never trained for sentence similarity, this measure mostly tracks text length. In 6.06 million Reddit comments, an uncentered DeBERTa-v3 measure had suggested that only conservative discourse broke toward homogeneity after late 2022. Truncating the same comments from 10 to 150 words raises their mean cosine by eight times the reported break. A placebo that swaps every comment for a random one of equal length reproduces 81% of the asymmetry, and a fixed-content simulation reproduces 78%. The leading principal direction carries 99.9% of raw DeBERTa homogeneity, and once length is handled the asymmetry disappears under every encoder. On 575,000 Stack Exchange answers the measure reports a post-ChatGPT homogenization of technical sites that the placebo fully reproduces, although answers grew longer. A census of 31 studies locates the risk where anisotropic encoders meet time-series or length-unequal designs. A reverse control on a well-known experiment shows that centering with renormalization can reverse a genuine effect. We propose a low-cost diagnostic protocol. Corrected measures show that the two political camps converged between 2019 and 2022 and stopped converging before ChatGPT. Cross-camp replies engage their targets more closely than same-camp replies.
title: Embedding Cosine Measures Text Length Before It Measures Homogenization

abstract: When AI agents relay information to one another, an output can preserve an injected instruction's effect on downstream agents even after its wording changes, yet legitimate quotation and template reuse can produce high textual overlap with the source, so text-similarity guardrails that attempt to flag the former risk conflating these two cases. We test this distinction using DonkeyRail, a public classifier combining BLEU, ROUGE-L, and METEOR features, deployed in a controlled three-agent email relay, defining a behavioral measure in which an output counts as functional (the injected procedure induces fresh computations in two subsequent agents) independent of the detector's score, alongside legitimate controls that explicitly authorize quotation and reuse. At its default threshold the classifier misses 8 of 19 functional outputs while flagging 70 of 192 legitimate replies, with every completed quotation and template-reuse reply triggering a false alert; calibrating for low false positives on one template set does not transfer, as the recalibrated threshold detects only one functional output and still produces 15 false alerts on new templates. We also identify an operating-point error in all 21 published classifier configurations, where ROC interpolation replaces direct threshold application, and show formally that high AUC against a surface-level text criterion provides no distribution-free guarantee of high AUC against the behavioral target, while the existing evaluation labels lack the joint observations needed to estimate the gap. An authorization analysis further shows that identical visible transcripts can require different safety decisions depending on the governing policy, a distinction no observation-only classifier can resolve. These results argue for behavioral and policy-grounded evaluation over text-similarity guardrails.
title: Safe Resemblance, Silent Propagation: Limits of Text-Similarity Guardrails for AI Agent Safety

abstract: Safe in-context reinforcement learning (Safe ICRL) asks a policy with fixed parameters to improve on an unseen constrained task from its interaction history while aiming to keep its cost within a budget. Prior work studied Safe ICRL on five benchmarks in three families: a grid world with a hidden goal and obstacles (DarkRoom), continuous navigation where goals and hazards stay invisible until reached (PointGoal, CarGoal), and locomotion with a hidden velocity limit (HalfCheetah, Ant). Safe Algorithm Distillation (Safe AD), trained on the learning histories of a safe RL algorithm, has shown adaptation failures in prior evaluations. For example, in the locomotion tasks its return stays below zero, and it rarely reaches the goal in CarGoal. We revisit two parts of Safe AD. First, we distill a budget-aware teacher with two phases. It searches for the hidden task, exploring more when more budget remains. After its first reward or cost, an expert policy exploits the task within the remaining budget. We collect the teacher's histories under fixed or dynamic budgets. Dynamic budgets increase the occupancy entropy of the return and budget inputs in every environment, and at test time they improve return and lower cost in DarkRoom and HalfCheetah. Second, we propose A-Lag, a test-time adjustment that reweights the distilled policy's actions by their predicted cost, with an adaptive Lagrange multiplier that is updated from the costs observed. In our experiments, A-Lag had lower mean episode cost than Safe AD in all five environments, with lower mean final return in four.
title: Algorithm Distillation for Safe In-Context Reinforcement Learning

abstract: When an authorization policy blocks an agent's tool call, the audit log should name the facts that forced the decision and nothing more. For an executable policy over an enumerable context space this minimal sufficient reason can be computed exactly, so an explanation is scored against ground truth rather than a proxy for it. We use that exactness to ask what a model can learn from a verifier that has no error in it. The explainer sees one request and one decision, never the policy, and has thirty turns in which it may call the policy on altered requests and ask whether a candidate set of facts is sufficient. Frontier models find the exact reason about half the time with the tools alone, and one sentence telling them to shrink the answer lifts Haiku 4.5 from 58% to 75%. A 4B model fine-tuned on 2000 traces of the deletion algorithm reaches 92% on the policy it was trained on. Teacher kind is what moves this: at matched data size the algorithm-taught student leads the frontier-taught one in all three training seeds, and the two arms never overlap. What the student learns is a fixed schedule of sufficiency checks, and the schedule does not travel. On three public policies it never saw, its answers stay sufficient (94%) and stop being minimal (48%), while Haiku under the same sentence is exact on all 47 episodes. Reinforcement learning from the exact reward leaves held-out accuracy where it was and inverts the strategy, from probing the policy to spending the entire budget on sufficiency checks. The oracle made the effect of training legible, but it did not make training better.
title: Procedure without Judgment: What Small Language Models Learn under an Exact Verifier

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to interpret, generate, and mediate public-facing language, which makes their reliability especially consequential in politically sensitive settings. Although sentiment analysis is a common task in this area, affective meaning in social media discourse is often conveyed through culturally situated and pragmatically indirect cues that are not well captured by label-centric evaluation alone. In this paper, we evaluate the robustness of LLMs for sentiment analysis of Spanish political discourse from social media, with emphasis on culturally situated affective interpretation. We introduce a diagnostic protocol that combines three independent human annotation views into Gold and Ambiguous subsets, and extends the corpus with a Synthetic subset built from sentiment-flipped counterfactuals selected through model-conditioned perplexity and LLM-as-a-judge criteria. Using this framework, we compare proprietary and open-weight models under zero-shot and few-shot prompting, focusing on predictive robustness across human agreement conditions and counterfactual shift. Our results show that annotation ambiguity and counterfactual perturbation reveal failure modes that conventional evaluation on the original corpus tends to obscure. GPT-4.1-mini remains the most stable among the evaluated models, whereas the two smaller open-weight models degrade more markedly under synthetic perturbations, and few-shot prompting provides only limited gains. Overall, the paper contributes a reproducible protocol for robustness-oriented evaluation in political sentiment analysis, an empirical characterization of model behavior under ambiguity and sentiment-flipped counterfactuals, and a publicly available Spanish social media dataset with three-way human sentiment annotations.
title: Evaluating Cultural Reasoning and Robustness in LLMs for Spanish Political Discourse

abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards inherits whatever its verifier gets wrong. Outside mathematics and code the verifier is a proxy, a rubric, a learned judge or a hand-written checker, and its distance from the true objective is never measured, so a rising reward cannot be told apart from a hack. We build a setting where the true reward is exactly computable at the process level: executable authorization policies over 124,416 contexts admit an oracle that lists every minimal sufficient reason for every decision. We compile these policies into exact process rewards, degrade the verifier along seven realistic axes (outcome-only, sufficiency, recall-only, extraction noise, coarse taxonomy, stale policy, LLM judge), and train against each while the exact verifier scores every rollout. Four phenotypes appear. Optimistic verifiers are hacked by padding: the sufficiency proxy ends at 0.940 while true faithfulness falls from 0.731 to 0.667 on 96 held-out episodes. Outcome-only verifiers saturate and stop teaching, noise dilutes, and ranking-preserving gaps do no harm. A model-free audit of the verifier, its selection error and gap sign, together with a short saturation pilot, anticipates which phenotype a run will produce. Across nine configurations spanning two frameworks, two model vendors, two adapter sizes, three precisions, two initialisations and two seeds, the phenotypes recur, sufficiency damage is positive in all 10 replication cells and beyond two standard errors in 7, and optimistic gaps remain the steeper branch. The damage magnitude does not replicate, and five pre-registered attempts to explain it are reported as they fell. We release the testbed, the training instrumentation, and 14 real public policies (Cedar, OPA, Gatekeeper) ported to executable oracles.
title: Optimistic Verifiers Get Hacked: Reward Hacking Under an Exact Process Oracle

abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) often fail to match a point or an object across two images, even when the answer can be decoded from their own hidden states. We trace this failure from the visual tokens to the answer letter, in Qwen3-VL (2B-32B), InternVL3.5-8B, and Gemma-3-12B, on synthetic shape matching, same-instance point correspondence (HPatches), and semantic correspondence (SPair-71k), and find two distinct failure points, a small set of attention heads that carries the comparison, and a repair that touches 0.02% of the parameters. Two failure points: exact copies are compared but not read out. An answer-position probe exceeds the calibrated output by 15 to 25 points in every family, for nameable and unnameable shapes alike, and steering along the probe's direction moves no more answers than random directions. Semantic correspondences are present in the visual tokens but never reach the answer. One pathway: redistributing the cross-image attention of 16-32 heads, with its mass preserved, removes 17-22 points of synthetic and 15-32 points of HPatches accuracy, against at most 7 for random or attention-matched heads. A lever that training finds on its own: training only these heads' query and key projections raises SPair-71k accuracy by 28.3 points (Qwen3-VL-8B) and 25.1 points (InternVL3.5-8B), beats both layer-matched and attention-matched heads, and transfers to HPatches and BLINK. An unconstrained all-layer adapter routes 21-51% of its gain through the attention of the same heads, against at most 7% for random heads, and does so by changing what they read (83-86% of the effect) rather than their weights. Every decision rule was frozen before its run, and every reported number is recomputed by independent verification scripts.
title: Seen but Unsaid: Locating and Repairing Cross-Image Comparison in Vision-Language Models

abstract: We introduce SciResearch-Eval, an interactive benchmark of scientific judgment built on a standard laboratory problem: measuring a material's thermal properties by heating it and fitting a heat-conduction simulator. An agent designs its own experiments, uses a supplied simulator that may be under-resolved or physically wrong, and reports each property with a 95% interval. To our knowledge it is the first benchmark to combine agent-designed experiments, a deliberately flawed simulator, and proper scoring of calibrated intervals against exact ground truth. On a held-out split (93 tasks, 9 models, 2,511 episodes), models handle procedural traps. When the simulator is missing physics, most report wrong values while stating they are 95% sure: their ranges contain the truth in 20-62% of cases, against 94% for GPT-6 Astra and 99% for Claude Fable 5.2. At default effort the failing Claude 5.5 models rarely diagnose the missing physics (Opus in 35% of episodes, against 66% for Astra), and even when they do, their ranges often miss; Astra and Fable design experiments in which the flawed simulator is accurate, such as gentle heating, which keeps Astra calibrated even when it does not name the cause. Asking for wider intervals does not help; stating the strategy improves interval scores 1.6-2.5-fold, replicated on a pre-registered fresh split, but coverage barely moves. A pre-registered effort ablation shows that the correction is latent in the Claude 5.5 models: at maximum effort Opus improves more than tenfold and is no longer detectably behind Astra at default, but only with 13-31 times more reasoning; older and open-weight models gain nothing. Fable 5.2 is the most accurate model at default effort (interval score 1.9 times better than Astra's) but writes 6 times as many tokens, and at Astra's token count it falls short. We release the environment, graders and harness.
title: SciResearch-Eval: Evaluating Scientific Judgment in Autonomous Experimental Agents

abstract: Consider an online prediction setting, where at each time, we are given a new feature vector and asked to provide a prediction interval or prediction set that will likely contain the corresponding response. In this setting, if the data points are i.i.d. (or more generally, exchangeable), conformal prediction provides a mechanism for building valid prediction sets around the output of any trained model, offering coverage probability $\geq 1-α$ at each time $t$. In practice, however, issues such as distribution drift, changepoints, or other challenges may cause violations of the i.i.d. assumption. In this adversarial setting, online conformal prediction methods can still offer guarantees on long-run empirical coverage.
